What FLUX saves, segment by segment

Savings are a property of your workload's shape. One global percentage would be a lie to someone; these are the four shapes, each with its mechanism, its measured band, and what would change the number. All figures simulator-measured per methodology; traceability in evidence.

Background / batch / latency-tolerant work — 57.7% net (64.3% ceiling)

Mechanism: your provider sells the same model at 50% off for work that can wait (OpenAI's flex service tier on a synchronous API; Anthropic's batches, which stack with prompt caching). FLUX applies the tier only to traffic you flag latency-tolerant, stacks it with every token lever below, and bills from the tier the provider *actually served* — bounced requests bill at full rate. The number to use is 57.7% (net of assumed 10% default-fallback + 5% retry rates); 64.3% is the zero-fallback ceiling. Quality: identical model, identical answers; 38/40 clean on the harness. What changes it: your real fallback rate (telemetry replaces the assumption), and Anthropic-side pricing once its batch rate is catalogued.

One-shot API traffic on a shared template — 45.5%, up to 72.8%

Mechanism: the most common silent waste we model: a per-request value (a timestamp, a request id) at the top of an otherwise identical prompt, which disables provider caching entirely. FLUX relocates it, the prefix caches at one-tenth price, and schema/duplicate levers stack on top. Add the tier for latency-tolerant one-shots and the band reaches 72.8%. What changes it: how big your shared template is and whether a breaker is actually present — the five-minute quote measures both from your export.

Interactive agents — 25.9–29.4% busy, 34.3% sparse

Mechanism: busy agent traffic is already heavily subsidised by the provider's cache (35–40% on its own, which we never claim), so FLUX's honest headroom is the *fresh* tokens: oversized tool results are capped at injection (headlines, errors and file paths preserved verbatim; the replay gate approved this lever at exactly zero quality delta), stale history is compacted byte-stably, schemas are slimmed. Sparse traffic adds the 1-hour cache TTL (2× write premium billed honestly, netted when negative) for 34.3%. What changes it: how oversized your tool results actually are (our fixture's are highly compressible; your yield scales with yours), and the pending per-model cache-minimum fix, which may lower the sparse figure on some models. On Claude the ceiling is different — and higher. Anthropic's prompt cache is opt-in, and agents that never place cache_control re-pay full rate for their whole conversation history every turn (our first live export measured exactly that: a five-turn agent with zero cache traffic). FLUX stamps the stable prefix with a 5-minute-TTL breakpoint. In the deterministic fixture, the cache-only comparison is 37.9% lower cost than the identical J prompt stack with caching disabled; both arms have 38/40 clean tasks and the stamp is metadata-only. The earlier 57.3% full-stack comparison used a raw uncached baseline with 40/40 clean tasks, while the candidate had 38/40 (−5 pp). That fails the agreed −2 pp quality limit, so 57.3% is diagnostic and not a qualified full-stack saving. Real-traffic cache validation remains open. If you already place your own breakpoints, FLUX defers and never claims this. This is also where we tell you our ceiling: if someone promises an interactive agent 70%, ask for their per-task evidence.

Always-on agents — where the compounding lives

An agent that never stops — an ops monitor, an autonomous worker, a multi-agent team running around the clock — re-buys its own memory on every single turn, forever. On real agent traffic we measured, each output token an agent emits is re-read roughly 27 more times as later turns re-send the history, and a well-cached agent's bill is ~52% cache reads. Two of our measured matrix shapes ARE always-on patterns: multi-agent teams at −55.6% cost and autonomous long-horizon agents at −40.0% (lossless levers plus the cache stamp, breakpoint-exact provider rules, simulator-measured).

The always-on trap is cadence. A busy loop (calls under five minutes apart) keeps the provider's 5-minute cache warm for free — every read refreshes the clock, and FLUX's stamp earns indefinitely. But an always-on agent that is *bursty* — polling every ten minutes, waiting on webhooks — silently expires its cache in every gap and re-pays the write premium on its whole history each time it wakes. FLUX's volatility and minimum guards already refuse the placements that lose money there; a cadence-aware TTL policy (choosing the 1-hour tier for prefixes whose observed gaps exceed five minutes) is in development and will be published with its own measured band, like everything else here.

What ships today for long-lived agents: correct, guarded cache placement; byte-stable history digests and the gated fresh-tool-result cap for unbounded context growth (real traces show tool results reaching 2,500–10,000 tokens at p99); exact-duplicate removal; byte-identical retry flagging (4–8% of real agent actions in public traces); and output-waste metering — on real agent trajectories, ~24% of output tokens re-emit text already in the context, and your statement shows your own number, measured, not billed. What changes it: your cadence (the gap histogram decides the cache economics) and your tool-result sizes.

Already-optimised stacks — 0–5%: do not pay us

Mechanism: none, and that is the point. If your input already arrives largely cached, or your gateway's response cache already answers a big share of requests, FLUX's triage says so and the quote's verdict is doNotPayUs. On our fixture of such a stack the addressable saving was 2.4%. A percentage-of-savings vendor that charges you for savings you already had is buying a dispute; we decline up front.
